title: Optimal size of four-additive graph spanners
formal: Determine \(s_{4}(n)=\max _{G} \min _{H} |E(H)|\) up to universal multiplicative constants for integers \(n\ge 2\), where G ranges over connected simple undirected unweighted graphs on n vertices and H ranges over their spanning subgraphs satisfying \(d_{H}(u,v)\le d_{G}(u,v)+4\) for all vertices u,v.
context:
The survey asks whether +4 error can be achieved with \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges, compared with the known exponent \(7/5\). This is a major gap in the sparsity of additive distance-preserving subgraphs.

The 2025 deterministic construction improves construction time while retaining the soft-\(O(n^{7/5})\) edge bound. The source does not supply an \(n^{4/3}\) upper bound.

Six-additive spanners achieve the \(4/3\) exponent, and general lower bounds obstruct beating that exponent for constant additive error. The +4 regime therefore asks whether a basic sparsity threshold can be reached with a smaller distance error.

The original \(O(n^{4/3})\) conjecture remains the candidate sharp upper bound; standard high-girth examples require \(\Omega (n^{4/3})\) edges. The retained question asks for the actual optimal size even if that conjecture fails. It is not asserted to be equivalent to the original yes/no question.

The question of how additive error must grow when only \(O(n)\) edges are allowed is separately retained as TCS-6785. This card keeps the important +4 regime, rather than bundling weighted, variable-error and failure-tolerant models.
why: The +4 additive-spanner regime is the classical remaining constant-error sparsity-exponent gap, making it a central distance-compression problem rather than a peripheral parameter choice.
status_note: The +4 sparsity gap remains in the 2025 primary source. The broader variable-error linear-size question is retained separately as TCS-6785.

sentences: An additive spanner keeps original graph edges while limiting the increase in every pairwise distance.
This card fixes the increase to at most four and asks for the optimal worst-case number of edges.
The target is the complete asymptotic function up to universal constant factors.
The familiar candidate is \(n^{4/3}\), while recent constructions still have exponent \(7/5\) up to logarithmic factors.
This gap is a fundamental unresolved regime of distance compression, and the variable-error linear-size tradeoff has its own card.

definitions: Each original edge has length one. \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path, with \(d_{G}(u,u)=0\). A spanning subgraph H has the same vertex set and a subset of G’s edges, with unchanged unit lengths. If u,v are disconnected in H put \(d_{H}(u,v)=\infty\), so the requirement forces H to be connected. The lower inequality \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) follows from being a subgraph. Both extrema exist because there are finitely many graphs on a fixed labeled vertex set and \(H=G\) is feasible. The cost is number of retained edges; neither construction time nor weights, shortcuts, missing vertices, terminal subsets or faults are part of the model. New weighted edges would be an emulator and are not allowed. Restricting to connected inputs only removes disconnected bookkeeping; applying a universal bound componentwise recovers its usual all-graph form.
answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(n)\), constants \(a,A>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that a \(g(n)\le s_{4}(n)\le A g(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\). Prove a universal existence upper bound and a matching worst-case lower bound. Polynomial exponents alone do not settle this constant-factor target if a growing logarithmic gap remains. This is an asymptotic extremal-size question, not an additive 0.01 estimate of an integer function.
